title: First 100 Users: The Quiet Art of Turning People Away

segments.text: This is First 100 Users, your late-night signal. Everything on tonight's shelf is about winning your first customers. Yet the strongest voices keep telling you who to ignore, and what not to do.
Start with the launch. You and I treat it as the big moment. But Paul Graham, writing on doing things that don't scale, just shrugs at the whole idea of it.
Think of some successful startups. How many of their launches do you remember?
segments.speaker: Paul Graham

segments.text: Now hear Rahul Vohra of Superhuman. Two years of coding, fourteen people, and still no launch, because throwing it out there felt wrong to him.
the "launch and see what happens" method seemed irresponsible and reckless to me
segments.speaker: Rahul Vohra, Superhuman

source.title: How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product Market Fit

segments.text: So two notes, in different rooms, quietly agree. The launch you're agonising over barely matters. What you do with the handful who actually show up matters far more.
Which opens a stranger question. Who do you serve? Graham says pour yourself into every early user, and feel no fear at all about overdoing it.
I have never once seen a startup lured down a blind alley by trying too hard to make their initial users happy.
segments.speaker: Paul Graham

segments.text: But Vohra, hunting product-market fit, says some users you should coldly turn your back on. Listen to how blunt he lets himself be.
Politely disregard those who would not be disappointed without your product. They are so far from loving you that they are essentially a lost cause.
segments.speaker: Rahul Vohra, Superhuman

source.title: How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product Market Fit

segments.text: And the Y Combinator talk on first customers nods along, telling you to cut people loose without flinching.
don't be afraid of letting customers go
segments.speaker: Gustav, Y Combinator Startup School

source.title: How to Get Your First Customers | Startup School
source.author: Y Combinator

segments.text: Feel the tension? Delight everyone, says one. Delight the right ones and release the rest, say the others. The quiet reconciliation is this. Lavish love, but only where it compounds.
Last thread, and the oddest one. The money itself. Pieter Levels, looking back on the whole digital nomad boom, spotted a pattern in exactly who survived it.
the bigger the bet financially the more financial engineering there is when it goes wrong and the higher odds you end up with the entire thing just disappearing into a black hole
segments.speaker: Pieter Levels (@levelsio)

source.title: The Rise and Fall of the Digital Nomad Startup Boom
source.author: @levelsio (@levelsio)

segments.text: And Vohra, deep inside venture-backed startup land, arrives at the very same warning, only he's facing it from the inside out.
Investors advising early-stage teams should avoid pushing for growth ahead of product-market fit.
segments.speaker: Rahul Vohra, Superhuman

source.title: How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product Market Fit

segments.text: So here's the question to carry into your next piece of work. Which of your users actually compound, and which just make noise on the way out?
And underneath that, a harder one. Are you funding patience, or buying pressure you'll spend years trying to outrun? Sleep on it. This has been First 100 Users.
